lenses.sp: Wants a large, steady, cheap company with a strong balance sheet.
lenses.vd: In Benjamin Graham's spirit: would see a mixed picture (2 checks use fewer years than the rule needs).

ch.r: Market value above ₹5,000 crore
ch.w: Graham avoided small companies; ₹5,000 crore is our Indian translation of 'adequate size'.

ch.r: Current assets ÷ current liabilities ≥ 2
ch.w: For every ₹100 it owes within a year, it holds ₹134 of cash, stock and dues coming in.

ch.r: Long-term debt ≤ current assets − current liabilities
ch.v: Long-term debt ₹261 cr vs working capital ₹985 cr
ch.w: Graham wanted the short-term cushion alone to be able to repay long-term loans.

ch.n: A profit every year for 10 years
ch.r: Positive earnings in each of the last 10 years
ch.v: Profit in all 4 yrs we have
ch.w: No loss in the years we can see; the earlier years are not in the free data.

ch.r: Dividends every year for 20 years (India: 10 years)
ch.w: A gap of about 35 months without a dividend (2019-09 to 2022-09).

ch.n: Earnings per share up a third in 10 years
ch.r: EPS +33% over 10 years (3-year averages at each end)
ch.w: EPS (average of the first 2 vs last 2 years we have) moved +43%.

ch.r: PE ≤ 15 on 3-year average earnings
ch.w: You pay ₹47 for every ₹1 of average yearly profit over the last 3 yrs.
You pay ₹7.91 for every ₹1 of net worth.

ch.r: Price < √(22.5 × EPS × book value per share)
ch.w: With EPS ₹47.2 and book value ₹191 per share, Graham's ceiling price is ₹450.

lenses.st: Wonderful business at a fair price
lenses.sp: Wants a simple business with a lasting edge, high returns without debt, and trustworthy managers.
lenses.vd: In Warren Buffett's spirit: a great business, and the price passes both this lens's own price test and the fair-value check (₹1,510 vs fair value ₹1,907).

ch.r: Could you explain how it makes money in two sentences?
q: What does it sell, and to whom?
Will people still need this in 10 years?

ch.r: A lasting edge: brand, low cost, network or switching costs
q: Why can't a well-funded rival copy it?
Has it kept high returns through bad years?

ch.r: ROE ≥ 15% in at least 8 of the last 10 years, with debt-to-equity < 0.5
ch.w: Strong in 4 of the 4 yrs we can see.

ch.r: No loss in 10 years
ch.w: No loss in the years we can see.

ch.n: Doesn't eat its cash in capex
ch.r: Capex < 50% of operating cash flow (5-year sum)

ch.r: Share count up no more than 5% over the years we have
ch.w: Your slice of the company hasn't been shrunk by new share issues.

ch.r: Candid, sensible with capital, no governance red flags
ch.v: No management red flags in our automatic checks (checked: auditor changes, CFO/KMP changes, credit ratings, SEBI orders, promoter holding, pledge).
ch.w: Our automatic checks are a starting point only.

story.what_it_does: APL Apollo makes steel tubes, mainly structural tubes, and sold about 3.5 million tonnes in FY26. Revenue was ₹230,790 Mn and net profit ₹12,031 Mn, and value-added products were 58% of sales.
story.plans: Management plans to raise capacity from about 5 million tonnes to 8 million tonnes by FY28, funded from internal cash. For FY27 it guides about 15% volume growth and about 20% absolute EBITDA growth, and expects the second half to beat the first half.
story.moat: The notes point to a large market share (65% in FY26) and a strong balance sheet, with net cash of ₹16.3 bn and zero working-capital days. EBITDA per tonne held above ₹5,500 even as volumes fell, which suggests pricing strength, though the notes do not explain the source of any lasting advantage.

scenarios.story: Volume recovers as the Q2 FY27 rebound (about 960,000 tonnes) continues and new capacity comes online. EBITDA per tonne reaches about ₹6,000 and absolute EBITDA hits the ₹2,200 crore target.
signals_to_watch: Q3 FY27 volume near the 10.5 lakh tonne target

scenarios.story: Volume growth lands near 15% and EBITDA grows about 20% for FY27, helped by higher per-tonne profit. Capacity expansion proceeds on cash the company already holds.

scenarios.story: The UAE disruption, steel shortages and soft demand continue to limit volumes, and management declines to commit to overall volume growth. Per-tonne profit could slip as light structures dilute the mix and aggressive pricing is used to win volume.
